claims.claim: The cortical location of an area was a good predictor of its connectivity in neonates.
claims.source: This indicates that the cortical location of an area was a good predictor of its connectivity; this is similar to what has been found in adult monkeys using within-hemisphere anatomical connections (Young, 1992; Markov et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the multidimensional scaling analysis, compared with previous studies in adults.

claims.claim: Spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlations partitioned 16 cortical areas into 3 groups: occipital areas V1, V2, and V3; ventral temporal areas V4, V4A, OTd, PITv, PITd, and OTS; and dorsal areas V3A/DP, CIP, LIP, as well as the MT cluster.
claims.source: Spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlations partitioned these 16 cortical areas into 3 groups: (1) occipital areas V1, V2, and V3 (green dots), (2) ventral temporal areas V4, V4A, OTd, PITv, PITd, and OTS (red dots), and (3) dorsal areas V3A/DP, CIP, LIP, as well as the MT cluster (blue dots).
claims.evidence: This is supported by spectral community structure analysis of neonatal correlation data.

claims.claim: MT was functionally grouped with dorsal stream areas despite its anatomical location in temporal cortex and proximity to ventral stream areas.
claims.source: Consistent with the organization found in adult monkeys, MT was functionally grouped with dorsal stream areas despite its anatomical location in temporal cortex and proximity to ventral stream areas V4, OTd, and PIT (Ungerleider and Mishkin, 1982).
claims.evidence: This is supported by community structure analysis and comparison with adult organization.

claims.claim: Occipital cortical areas were correlated with both ventral and dorsal groups.
claims.source: Occipital cortical areas were correlated with both ventral and dorsal groups.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the community structure analysis.

claims.claim: Correlations between dorsal and ventral groups were present, though relatively weak compared to correlations within groups.
claims.source: Correlations between dorsal and ventral groups were also present, though relatively weak compared to correlations within groups.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the correlation analysis.

claims.claim: There is a clear distinction, at birth, between dorsal and ventral visual pathways, which is similar to the known organization of the adult visual system.
claims.source: This analysis thus yielded a clear distinction, at birth, between dorsal and ventral visual pathways, which is similar to the known organization of the adult visual system.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the community structure analysis, compared with adult organization.

claims.claim: Hierarchical cluster analysis revealed nested layers within the functional segregation of dorsal and ventral pathways at birth.
claims.source: Hierarchical cluster analysis revealed nested layers within the functional segregation of dorsal and ventral pathways at birth (Figure 5b).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5b.

claims.claim: V1 was situated in the middle of the dendrogram with one set of areas extending into inferior temporal cortex and other areas extending into parietal cortex.
claims.source: V1 was situated in the middle of the dendrogram with one set of areas (left) extending into inferior temporal cortex and other areas (right) extending into parietal cortex.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the hierarchical clustering analysis.

claims.claim: Hierarchical clustering resulted in a finer-grained parcellation into five clusters: posterior occipital areas V1, V2, and V3; anterior occipital areas V4, V4A, and OTd; inferior temporal areas PITd, PITv, and OTS; the MT cluster; and dorsal areas V3A, CIP, LIP.
claims.source: Hierarchical clustering resulted in a finer-grained parcellation into five clusters: posterior occipital areas V1, V2, and V3 (green), anterior occipital areas V4, V4A, and OTd (peach), inferior temporal areas PITd, PITv, and OTS (red), the MT cluster (cyan), and dorsal areas V3A, CIP, LIP (blue).
claims.evidence: This is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of neonatal correlation data.

claims.claim: The multidimensional scaling and hierarchical clustering revealed the presence, at birth, of the well-established (in adults) broad differentiation between dorsal and ventral visual pathways as well as a hierarchical organization within each pathway.
claims.source: Taken together, the multidimensional scaling and hierarchical clustering revealed the presence, at birth, of the well-established (in adults) broad differentiation between dorsal and ventral visual pathways as well as a hierarchical organization within each pathway.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the community structure and hierarchical clustering analyses.

claims.claim: A series of retinotopic representations could be inferred from correlation patterns in neonatal visual areas.
claims.source: An even finer level of differentiation within individual neonatal visual areas was apparent as a series of retinotopic representations that could be inferred from correlation patterns.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of neonatal fMRI data.

claims.claim: Within-hemisphere correlations between dorsal or ventral quadrant pairs were stronger than correlations between non-matched quadrant pairs.
claims.source: Within-hemisphere correlations between dorsal or ventral quadrant pairs (e.g., dorsal V1 and dorsal V2) were stronger than correlations between non-matched quadrant pairs (2-way ANOVA; main effects of quadrant group: F(1,156) = 45.1, p<0.0001; marginal effect of monkey F(1,156)=3.63, p<0.06; no interaction p>0.10)
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of within-hemisphere correlation data.

claims.claim: The mean signals of homotopic quadrants across hemispheres were significantly correlated in each monkey.
claims.source: The mean signals of homotopic quadrants across hemispheres were significantly correlated in each monkey (ts(9)>17.21; ps<0.001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of across-hemisphere correlation data.

claims.claim: The homotopic correlations were stronger for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants.
claims.source: The checkerboard pattern of the correlation matrix in Figure 6a indicates that the homotopic correlations were stronger for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants (Figure 6b; 2-way ANOVA with monkey and quadrant group as factors; p<0.0001).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of correlation data shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Across-hemisphere correlations between non-homotopic regions were greater for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants than for non-corresponding quadrants.
claims.source: Across-hemisphere correlations between non-homotopic regions were also greater for corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants (e.g., dorsal V1 right hemisphere to dorsal V3 left hemisphere) than for non-corresponding quadrants (2-way ANOVA; main effect of quadrant group: F(1,92) = 10.87, p<0.0014; no main effect of monkey, p>0.10; no interaction between monkey and quadrant group, p>0.10).
claims.evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of across-hemisphere correlation data.

claims.claim: Dorsal:dorsal and ventral:ventral correlations were stronger than dorsal:ventral correlations even across areas, likely reflecting the underlying topographic organization within each area.
claims.source: Because dorsal:dorsal and ventral:ventral correlations were stronger than dorsal:ventral correlations even across areas (e.g., V1 to V3), these correlations likely reflect the underlying topographic organization within each area, not solely mirror symmetrical point-to-point connections between hemispheres.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the correlation data about the nature of the organization.

claims.claim: Callosal connections linking neurons with overlapping receptive fields at or near the vertical meridian can account for correlated activity between hemispheres in adults.
claims.source: Even though right and left hemispheres represent left and right visual fields, respectively, callosal connections linking neurons with overlapping receptive fields at or near the vertical meridian (Dehay et al., 1986) can account for correlated activity between hemispheres in adults (Heinzle et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claims.claim: A coarse topographic organization within individual areas of newborn monkeys likely reflects retinotopic organization.
claims.source: These data demonstrate a coarse topographic organization within individual areas of newborn monkeys that likely reflects retinotopic organization.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the quadrant correlation analysis.

claims.claim: The IC analysis revealed a broad foveal vs. peripheral distinction in neonates.

claims.evidence: This is supported by ICA analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The checkerboard pattern of correlations between dorsal vs. ventral subdivisions of individual occipital areas indicated a lower vs. upper visual-field specificity.
claims.source: and the checkerboard pattern of correlations between dorsal vs. ventral subdivisions of individual occipital areas (Figure 6) indicated a lower vs. upper visual-field specificity.
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6.

claims.claim: Within-hemisphere correlated activity patterns at early age reflected the retinotopic organization measured in the same monkeys much later in life.

claims.claim: The eccentricity correlation maps obtained in neonates were predictive of the eccentricity organization derived by direct retinotopic mapping in the same monkeys when they were older.

claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal eccentricity correlation maps with later retinotopic mapping shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Lateral occipital cortex had foveal correlations in neonates that extended anteriorly along the lower lip of the STS.
claims.source: Specifically, lateral occipital cortex had foveal correlations in neonates that extended anteriorly along the lower lip of the STS.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Moving towards the medial occipital surface, eccentricity correlations gradually shifted towards the periphery.
claims.source: Moving towards the medial occipital surface, eccentricity correlations gradually shifted towards the periphery.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claims.claim: A region of foveal correlation, distinct from the foveal confluence of early visual cortex, was present within the fundus of the STS, corresponding to what later could be identified as the fovea of the MT cluster.
claims.source: A region of foveal correlation, distinct from the foveal confluence of early visual cortex, was present within the fundus of the STS, corresponding to what later could be identified as the fovea of the MT cluster.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with later mapping.

claims.claim: Parafoveal and peripheral correlations encircled the MT fovea, especially in the dorsal-most portions of the STS near the prelunate gyrus and crown of the IPS, consistent with the retinotopic organization identified when the monkeys were older.
claims.source: Parafoveal and peripheral correlations encircled this fovea, especially in the dorsal-most portions of the STS near the prelunate gyrus and crown of the IPS; consistent with the retinotopic organization identified when the monkeys were older.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with later mapping.

claims.claim: The mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations in newborns and the eccentricity measurements from retinotopic mapping after 1.5 years of age was 2.2° across all retinotopic areas (excluding V1).
claims.source: Excluding V1 (i.e., the seed area), the mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations in newborns and the eccentricity measurements from retinotopic mapping after 1.5 years of age was 2.2° across all retinotopic areas, in both hemispheres, in both monkeys.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neonatal correlation maps with later retinotopic mapping.

claims.claim: Actual V1 correlations with V2 and V3 were approximately 2x and 5x, respectively, greater than estimated correlations attributable to spatial spread of the fMRI signal.
claims.source: Actual V1 correlations with V2 and V3 were approximately 2x and 5x, respectively, greater than estimated correlations attributable to spatial spread of the fMRI signal.
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of actual correlations with simulated correlations from spatial spread.

claims.claim: Anterior to V3, correlations with V1 in the simulation were negligible.
claims.source: Anterior to V3, correlations with V1 in our simulation were negligible.
claims.evidence: This is a result from the simulation analysis.

claims.claim: The neonate eccentricity correlation maps were similar to correlation maps obtained in the same monkeys as juveniles (~3 years of age).
claims.source: The neonate eccentricity correlation maps were also similar to correlation maps obtained in the same monkeys as juveniles (~3 years of age), indicating that retinotopic correlation patterns are present through development.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal and juvenile correlation maps.

claims.claim: The mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations at newborn and juvenile ages was 2.0° across retinotopic areas (excluding V1).
claims.source: Excluding V1, the mean absolute deviation between eccentricity correlations at newborn and juvenile ages was 2.0° across retinotopic areas, in both hemispheres, in both monkeys.
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative comparison of neonatal and juvenile correlation maps.

claims.evidence: This is a comparison of juvenile correlations with both neonatal correlations and later mapping, suggesting developmental refinement.

claims.claim: Extensive retinotopic organization across both early and higher visual cortex was already present within the first weeks of life.
claims.source: These data indicate that extensive retinotopic organization across both early and higher visual cortex was already present within the first weeks of life.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the eccentricity correlation analysis.

claims.claim: Early eccentricity maps extended into regions of IT cortex that in adults are organized into domains selectively responsive to different object categories, like faces.
claims.source: These early eccentricity maps extended into regions of IT cortex that in adults are organized into domains selectively responsive to different object categories, like faces (Tsao et al., 2003; Pinsk et al., 2009; Bell et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis, compared with adult organization.

claims.claim: Regions of IT selectively responsive to face and non-face stimuli (measured with fMRI) were not differentiable in IT cortex at young age.
claims.source: At this young age, however, regions of IT selectively responsive to face and non-face stimuli (measured with fMRI) were not differentiable in IT cortex (Livingstone et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a previous study from the same lab.

claims.claim: Face patches would not emerge until about 200 days in these monkeys.
claims.source: Face patches would not emerge until about 200 days in these monkeys (Figure 8a, thick black outline).

claims.claim: Foveal biases were identified in neonatal data along the lower lip of the STS, including a region that would eventually be identifiable as the middle face patch (ML).
claims.source: Yet foveal biases were identified in this neonatal data along the lower lip of the STS, including a region that would eventually be identifiable as the middle face patch (ML), consistent with previous studies that compared eccentricity and face patch organization in adult monkeys (Janssens et al., 2014; Rajimehr et al., 2014; Lafer-Sousa and Conway, 2013).

claims.claim: In neonates, the eccentricity correlations within what would become area ML were mostly foveal, though midfield and peripheral representations were identified on the medial edge within the fundus in 3 of 4 hemispheres.

claims.evidence: This is an observation from the eccentricity correlation analysis in the precursor-ML region.

claims.claim: The progression of eccentricity representations in the precursor-ML region was consistent with eccentricity representations from subsequent mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years of age, and with a previous study in adult monkeys.

claims.claim: Correlations of the region that would become ML were strongest with the most foveal V1 bin and diminished towards the periphery.

claims.evidence: This is supported by analysis of correlations between precursor-ML and V1 eccentricity bins shown in Figure 8b.

claims.claim: The pattern of V1 eccentricity correlations in neonates paralleled the distribution of eccentricity representations in ML from subsequent retinotopic mapping in these same monkeys at >1.5 years; both showed an overall foveal bias.

claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of neonatal correlations with later retinotopic mapping shown in Figure 8b and c.

claims.claim: The anterior face patch (AL) showed a bimodal retinotopic correlation pattern, with the strongest correlations at foveal- and peripheral-most V1 bins.

claims.claim: Retinotopic organization of what would become category-selective regions in IT cortex was already established within the first weeks after birth.
claims.source: Together, these data indicate that retinotopic organization of what would become category-selective regions in IT cortex was already established within the first weeks after birth.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the analysis of eccentricity correlations in precursor face-patch regions.

claims.claim: Neonatal correlation patterns did not reveal a face-patch organization.
claims.source: Though neonatal correlation patterns distinguished retinotopic areas within IT (Figures 2 and 4) and neonatal ICA analysis revealed a broad IT component (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), neither analysis revealed a face-patch organization in neonates.

claims.claim: The retinotopic areal organization in inferior temporal cortex precedes category selectivity.

claims.claim: The mean preferred spatial frequency decreased moving up the hierarchy, in both dorsal and ventral pathways.

claims.claim: There is a correlation between eccentricity and spatial frequency in infants prior to the emergence of category selectivity.
claims.source: Thus, although we could not do spatial frequency mapping in neonatal monkeys, we nevertheless did observe a correlation between eccentricity and spatial frequency in infants that were slightly older but still prior to the emergence of category selectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion from the spatial frequency mapping in 110-day-old infant.

claims.claim: The presence of retinotopy, as measured by correlation patterns in the neonates, implies a corresponding early organization for receptive field scale.
claims.source: We therefore assume that the presence of retinotopy, as measured by correlation patterns in the neonates, implies a corresponding early organization for receptive field scale.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between retinotopy and spatial frequency tuning.

claims.claim: Curvature selectivity varies with eccentricity in adult monkeys.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that hierarchical, topographic organization of the visual system is present at birth in neonatal macaques (10-18 days postnatal). Visual cortex was functionally distinct from other sensory regions, with arealization and hierarchical organization revealed through across-hemisphere correlations, and correlations between areas were retinotopically organized.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C8, C13, C115-C118, and C121 collectively establish the main finding through multiple converging lines of evidence: correlation analyses (C8, C15-C17), ICA analyses (C21-C24), seed-based correlation analyses (C25, C30-C39), community structure analyses (C40-C51), and retinotopic correlation patterns (C52-C74). The use of across-hemisphere correlations to avoid spatial spread artifacts (C33-C34) and validation with later retinotopic mapping (C62-C63, C68) strengthen the conclusions. Statistical significance is reported throughout (e.g., C30, C32, C35).

results.result: During the first few weeks after birth, visually evoked fMRI responses were largely absent except in LGN and peripheral V1, yet correlated activity between visual areas was significant and distinguished visual cortex from other regions. This dissociation may reflect population-level immaturity or low-arousal states rather than absence of functional organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C18 provide converging evidence from visually-evoked and resting-state fMRI data at different postnatal ages. The lack of early visually-evoked activity (C14) contrasts with significant correlations (C15-C16), which were verified by later retinotopic mapping (C17-C18). The proposed explanations (C19-C20) are appropriately framed as inferences based on comparison with previous studies using different methods, acknowledging alternative interpretations.

results.result: Independent component analysis revealed functionally specific regional differentiation within the visual system and throughout sensory cortex in neonates, with bilateral and symmetric spatial maps encompassing comparable regions between hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C24 describe ICA results showing multiple visual cortical components (foveal/peripheral occipital, dorsal extrastriate, MT, IT) and components in other sensory regions. The bilateral symmetry (C22) and regional specificity (C23-C24) are consistent with the correlation analyses and provide independent validation of early functional organization. The method is established in adults and appropriately applied to neonatal data.

results.result: Individual visual areas across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortices could be distinguished at birth using seed-based correlation analysis. Across-hemisphere correlations were strongest between homotopic areas, followed by adjacent areas, then distal areas, with control analyses ruling out instrumental artifacts.
results.evaluation: Claims C25, C30-C39 provide detailed evidence for arealization using across-hemisphere correlations to avoid spatial spread artifacts. Statistical analyses show significant correlations for all 16 areas (C30, C35), with systematic variation by areal grouping (C31-C32). Control simulations (C33-C34) demonstrate that observed correlations cannot be attributed to instrumentation or preprocessing. The areal correlation profile analysis (C37-C39) provides additional spatial specificity.

results.result: Community structure and hierarchical clustering analyses revealed organization of the neonatal visual system into dorsal and ventral pathways, with nested hierarchical organization within each pathway similar to adult organization. MT was functionally grouped with dorsal areas despite its temporal location.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C51 describe multiple complementary analyses (multidimensional scaling, spectral community structure, hierarchical clustering) that converge on the same organizational principles. The two-dimensional structure (posterior-anterior, dorsal-ventral; C41) and the functional grouping of MT with dorsal areas (C44) match known adult organization. The hierarchical clustering (C48-C50) reveals nested organization with appropriate metrics (cophenetic correlation = 0.83; C50). The modularity is modest (Q = 0.11) but significant.

results.result: Retinotopic organization was present within individual visual areas in neonates, as demonstrated by stronger correlations between corresponding dorsal or ventral quadrants (representing upper/lower visual fields) than between non-corresponding quadrants, both within and across hemispheres.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C61 provide evidence for coarse retinotopic organization through quadrant-based correlation analyses. Statistical analyses show significant effects for both within-hemisphere (C53) and across-hemisphere (C54-C56) correlations, with the checkerboard pattern (C55, C61) indicating visual field specificity. The across-hemisphere analysis rules out spatial spread artifacts. The interpretation that correlations reflect topographic organization rather than just mirror-symmetrical connections (C57) is supported by the pattern of results.

results.result: Detailed eccentricity organization was present across visual cortex in neonates, as demonstrated by V1 eccentricity-based correlation maps that predicted later retinotopic mapping (mean deviation 2.2°). These patterns were stable through development (mean deviation 2.0° between neonatal and juvenile), with evidence for refinement over time.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C74 provide strong evidence for detailed retinotopic organization through comparison of neonatal correlation maps with later conventional retinotopic mapping in the same animals. The quantitative agreement (2.2° mean deviation; C68) is impressive given the methodological differences. Control analyses show correlations exceed those expected from spatial spread (C69-C70). The developmental comparison (C71-C73) suggests both stability and refinement. The extension to higher visual areas including MT (C66-C67) is particularly notable.

results.result: Retinotopic organization in regions that would become face-selective patches in IT was present at birth (with foveal bias in precursor-ML region), months before face-selective clusters emerged at ~200 days. ICA and univariate analyses confirmed absence of face-patch organization before 200 days but presence after.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C90 provide compelling longitudinal evidence that retinotopic organization precedes category selectivity. The foveal bias in precursor-ML (C78-C82) matches later face-patch organization, with quantitative correlation profiles (C81-C82). The bimodal pattern in precursor-AL (C83) also matches later organization. The negative results for face-patch organization before 200 days (C85-C87) using both ICA and univariate methods strengthen the conclusion that retinotopy precedes category selectivity. The consistency of retinotopic ICs across ages (C88-C89) demonstrates stability.

results.result: Spatial frequency tuning varied as a function of both visual hierarchy and eccentricity in 110-day-old infants (prior to face-patch emergence), with foveal regions preferring higher spatial frequencies and mean preferred spatial frequency decreasing up the hierarchy in both dorsal and ventral pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C98 describe spatial frequency mapping at 110 days showing adult-like organization of spatial frequency tuning with eccentricity and hierarchy. The systematic variation with eccentricity (C96) and hierarchy (C97) is clearly demonstrated. The timing (after visual responses appear but before face patches emerge; C94) is appropriate for testing the hypothesis. The inference that neonatal retinotopy implies early receptive field scale organization (C99) is reasonable given the established relationship between eccentricity and spatial frequency tuning.

results.result: Curvature tuning varied as a function of area and eccentricity in 186-day-old infants (around face-patch emergence), with foveal regions in V1-V4A, OTd, and PITd preferring curved stimuli. Scene-selective regions (PITv, V3A/DP, OTS) showed preference for rectilinear stimuli, suggesting low-level shape selectivity precedes and contributes to category selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C114 describe curvature mapping at 186 days showing organization of low-level shape selectivity. The correlation with eccentricity (C103, C105) and the differential preferences in scene-selective regions (C107-C113) are consistent with adult organization. The timing (around face-patch emergence; C102) is appropriate. The conclusion that low-level shape selectivity precedes category selectivity (C114) is supported by the data, though the temporal relationship is less clear than for spatial frequency since measurements were made around the time of face-patch emergence rather than clearly before.

results.result: The organization observed at 10 days postnatal is unlikely to have emerged postnatally through visually driven activity; given axonal growth rates (0.4-1.4 mm/day), the wiring must have begun prenatally, establishing the large-scale organization prior to visual experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123, C126 provide a logical inference about the prenatal origins of the observed organization. The calculation based on axonal growth rates (C123) and the extent of organization at 10 days (C121) make postnatal emergence through visual experience unlikely. This is consistent with previous anatomical studies showing prenatal development of connections (C125). However, the inference relies on assumptions about the timing and extent of wiring required, and the authors appropriately acknowledge that mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study (C127).

results.result: Despite functional organization being apparent at birth, the visual system remains anatomically and functionally immature by several criteria. The organization found in neonates constitutes a proto-architecture that undergoes subsequent maturation and refinement through postnatal visual experience, as evidenced by the malleability of both V1 and IT to early experience.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C135 address the apparent paradox of early organization despite immaturity. The argument is well-supported by citations showing both adult-like features (C130) and immaturity/malleability (C131, C133-C134) of neonatal visual cortex. The conclusion that early organization constitutes a proto-architecture (C135) appropriately reconciles these observations. The comparison with V1 (C130-C131) provides a useful framework for interpreting extrastriate findings (C132). The evidence for refinement (C73) supports the proto-architecture interpretation.

results.result: Neonatal monkeys exhibited hierarchically organized retinotopic maps with increasing receptive field scale up the hierarchy (as indicated by decreasing spatial frequency preference), providing scaffolding for hierarchical computations thought to support object recognition.
results.evaluation: Claims C136-C143 synthesize findings about hierarchical organization of retinotopic maps. The evidence for retinotopy along both polar angle and eccentricity dimensions (C138) and the increasing receptive field scale up the hierarchy (C142, inferred from spatial frequency data C97) support the conclusion. The comparison with adult organization (C139-C140) and the inference about computational scaffolding (C143) are appropriate. However, the spatial frequency data are from 110 days, not neonates, so the inference about neonatal receptive field scale (C141-C142) involves extrapolation.

results.result: The authors propose that retinotopic proto-organization in IT serves as scaffolding for subsequent category-selective organization because it carries shape-based organization (faces are curved, scenes are rectilinear) and/or because of differential viewing behavior (foveating faces but not scenes).
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C154 present the main hypothesis about how early retinotopic organization scaffolds later category selectivity. The hypothesis is supported by: (1) correspondence between foveal bias and face selectivity in adults (C144), (2) foveal bias in precursor face regions at birth (C146), (3) spatial frequency and curvature tuning before face patches emerge (C147), and (4) differential shape properties of faces vs. scenes (C150). The proposal appropriately acknowledges two potential mechanisms (shape-based and viewing behavior; C154) and is framed as a hypothesis rather than proven fact. The evidence is consistent with but does not definitively prove the hypothesis.

results.result: The authors propose that retinotopic organization emerges early in development through molecular cues and self-organizing principles, serving as scaffolding for experience-dependent specialization. This may be a general principle extending to other sensory areas and possibly all of cortex, as suggested by somatotopic organization also being apparent in newborn data.
results.evaluation: Claims C155-C156 present broad proposals about developmental principles. While the visual system data strongly support the scaffolding role of early topographic organization (C155), the extension to other sensory areas and all of cortex (C156) is more speculative. The observation of somatotopic organization in neonatal data (C156) provides some support, but this is mentioned only briefly without detailed analysis. The proposal about mechanisms (molecular cues and self-organizing principles; C155) is acknowledged as beyond the scope of the study (C127). These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but go beyond what the current data definitively demonstrate.

results.result: The methodological approach of using across-hemisphere homotopic correlations is validated by previous anatomical and fMRI studies showing callosal connections between homotopic visual areas that are correlated with areal and hierarchical organization.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C29 establish the methodological foundation for using across-hemisphere correlations. The approach is well-validated by extensive citations to anatomical studies in both adult and infant primates (C26-C27) and previous fMRI studies (C28-C29). This provides strong justification for the analytical approach and interpretation of homotopic correlations as reflecting areal organization.

results.result: The data provide the developmentally earliest account of global functional organization of the visual system, demonstrating substrates for adult organization across the whole visual system, not just V1.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 assert the novelty and scope of the findings. The claim of providing the earliest account (C119) is supported by the young age of subjects (10 days) and the comprehensive nature of the analysis. The claim about demonstrating organization across the whole visual system (C120) is supported by the extensive mapping of 16 areas across occipital, temporal, and parietal cortex, going beyond previous studies focused on V1. The comparison with previous work (C120) appropriately acknowledges prior contributions while highlighting the advance.
